newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Europe can withstand 25 bp Fed rise.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Europe can withstand 25 bp Fed rise.

text.p: European bonds, immersed in issues closer to home and insulated by growing liquidity, will quickly ride out any short-term tremors caused by a 25 basis point rise in U.S. interest rates, analysts said on Tuesday.
While European markets would initially dip, they would soon outperform Treasuries against a backdrop of low interest rates and growing enthusiasm for European monetary union, they said.
"The curves are just so steep in Germany and other parts of Europe that the decoupling theme will remain intact," said Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London.
Opinion was slightly swayed towards expecting an interest rate rise after the policy-setting arm of the Federal Reserve meets later on Tuesday, analysts said.

In a survey by Reuters, 17 out of 30 economist predicted a rise in the 5.25 percent federal funds rate. All but one saw a 25 basis point increase. Only one firm saw a 0.50 increase and that firm also saw a 0.50 rise in the 5.0 percent discount rate.
Analysts said while both Treasuries and European bonds are likely to absorb a 25 basis point increase without too much pain, T-bonds face greater uncertainty as the year progresses.

"Once the rate hike is in place then the market will start to look for a lot more, and the debate will shift to how much rates will have to go up," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase in London. "There's clearly a risk that if we get some strong data coming through the whole (Treasury) market will go into a bit of a state of panic."
European bonds, meanwhile, have a much clearer horizon.
First and foremost, interest rates in the core European countries are unlikely to climb any time soon, while rates in high-yielding markets like Italy are set to drop, they said.
"Inflation and the businsess cycle in general will continue to support (European outperformance)," said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London.
He said there was even potential for the German Bundesbank to trim its 3.0 percent repo rate further, with consumer prices subdued and deflation in producer, wholesale and import prices.
Sanwa's Shah said European markets will also be protected by growing inflows of both domestic and international money.

"All European markets are basking in their own liquidity," he said. French bond markets, dominated by local investors, have received an additional boost from tax changes encouraging insurance companies to invest.
Foreign investments are growing too, he said.
"Easier monetary policy is helping the international community to maintain leveraged positions in the bond market because there is a tremendous positive carry," Shah said.
European bond markets will also continue to be preoccupied with convergence trades ahead of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), while Treasuries wrestle with the inflation beast.
High-yielding markets have outperformed dramatically this year as yields of peripheral bond markets converge against core markets like Bunds in anticipation of EMU starting in 1999.
"At the end of the day these convergence trades are perdominating and I would expect that to outweigh any influence from the U.S.," said Gunner.
Against this positive backdrop, Gunner saw the gap between the yield on 10-year Treasuries and German Bunds widening to 100 basis points from 75 in the next three months.
While analysts said European markets would be dragged under if the Fed hit the market with a 50 basis point rise, they said when the fuss had died down, Europe would outperform.
"My feeling is we will go to 90," said Shah of the T-notes/Bund spread. "The pace depends on the size of the rise."
If the Fed raises rates by 25 basis points, the spread would take a while to move to 90, he said. But a 0.50 rise would see it shoot out in a matter of days.
